answers.answer: CAP describes computers communicating over a network, with data copies held on different computers (the lesson illustrates two servers holding the same value). During a network split that prevents exchange, the system cannot guarantee both latest-data consistency and successful completion of every request. Choosing any two letters at all times is misleading because the forced consistency/availability choice is conditional on a partition; outside partitions CAP does not force that choice. A partition breaks message exchange between parts of the system; it does not require all nodes to crash. Both sides may remain running and receive client requests. Partition tolerance means accounting for those communication failures, not promising every operation is available. Omitting partitions from a discussion cannot restore connections or remove failures in the deployment.

evidence.quote: Uses computers that communicate over a network.
Prevents parts of a system from exchanging messages. Servers on both sides can still be running and receiving requests.
Means the design accounts for these communication failures. It does not promise that every operation remains available.
Two servers hold the value 10. Their connection breaks.
Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability.

answers.answer: CAP consistency is linearizability: operations fit one valid single-copy order respecting real time. With no intervening write, a read begun after a write completed must observe that write. Overlapping operations may appear in either valid order; globally synchronized request timestamps are not required. Eventual convergence permits temporarily older copies; ACID consistency preserves defined database rules rather than requiring this real-time read behavior. CAP availability means every valid request reaching a working node eventually succeeds. It imposes neither instantaneous responses nor a practical latency target. Refusal or an error does not complete the requested operation successfully, so it sacrifices availability even if it protects consistency. Uptime percentage measures a different thing from eventual success for every such request.

evidence.quote: Linearizability: operations behave as if they take effect in a single order that respects real time.
If a write completes before a read begins, and no intervening write changes the value, the read must reflect that write.
Overlapping operations may be placed in either order, provided the resulting order is valid for one copy.
This differs from eventual convergence and from ACID consistency, which concerns preserving defined database rules.
Means every valid request that reaches a working server eventually gets a successful result.
CAP availability does not mean fast, immediately answered, or a particular uptime percentage. The theorem requires eventual per-request completion and sets no practical response-time target.
An error response is not successful completion of the requested operation.

answers.answer: B knows its old value 0 and cannot learn the completed write at A through the broken connection. Consistency requires its later read to return 1 because no later write changed that value. Returning 0 completes the read but violates consistency. Refusing it or waiting indefinitely avoids an incorrect old result but fails eventual successful completion, hence availability. Guessing 1 happens to work for this write, but cannot guarantee correctness across different unseen writes; B lacks the information needed to distinguish their values.

evidence.quote: B cannot know about a change that no message can deliver.
If a write completes before a read begins, and no intervening write changes the value, the read must reflect that write.
The read succeeds, but breaks consistency.
B avoids returning old data, but cannot guarantee availability.
Guessing the new value cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen writes.

answers.answer: To preserve consistency during a partition, continue only safely coordinated operations that maintain a valid real-time order; affected reads or writes must wait or fail when that cannot be assured. This need not stop every node: in the lesson majority-based three-server protocol, a connected pair can commit while the isolated server cannot commit alone. To preserve availability, separated live sides keep accepting requests with their available information, giving up the guarantee that later reads reflect every completed write. A stale read returns an older state; conflicting writes are different accepted changes to the same item on separated sides. After recovery, exchange changes and merge, select one, or seek resolution of conflicts. Continuing requests does not guarantee safe merges, preservation of every accepted edit or its intent, or cross-record rules; those require explicit policies and protection.

evidence.quote: Preserves consistency during a partition. Some requests must wait or fail.
If the network splits into two servers and one, the connected pair can continue committing writes. The isolated server cannot commit writes on its own.
Safely coordinated operations can continue; favoring consistency need not shut down every part of the system.
Keeps accepting requests during a partition. Each side works with the information it has.
Reads can return older data. If both sides accept writes, they can produce conflicting changes to the same item.
After communication returns, the system exchanges changes. It needs a rule to merge them, select one, or ask someone to resolve the conflict.
Availability supplies no automatic safe merge. Selecting one conflicting value can lose another user's intent, and cross-record rules require their own protection.

answers.answer: Eventual consistency means copies converge when new updates stop, communication resumes, and required updates and reconciliation reach every copy. It guarantees neither a fixed deadline nor immediate read-your-writes, and convergence does not preserve every concurrent intent: the resolution policy chooses the resulting state. An operation requiring no value older than a completed write should serve only when it can maintain that order; during a split affected operations may wait or fail. On recovery it must still return the completed write or newer, coordinating before serving if needed. An operation allowing temporary old values can keep answering from reachable local copies during a split; clients can see staleness, and independently accepted writes may conflict. After recovery exchange changes and apply an explicit merge/selection/human-resolution policy; convergence follows under the stated conditions, possibly discarding an intent. Different operations in one database can offer different read guarantees, so choose/configure the guarantee per operation instead of treating a vendor label as permanent behavior. CAP alone does not decide ordinary latency, capacity, or cost. Gap: the lesson states that databases can offer different guarantees but gives no concrete configuration procedure.

evidence.quote: Copies converge if new updates stop, communication resumes and the required updates and reconciliation reach every copy.
Convergence means agreement on a resulting state. It does not promise that every conflicting edit survives; the conflict-resolution policy determines the result.
Eventually gives no fixed deadline or immediate read-your-writes guarantee.
Preserves consistency during a partition. Some requests must wait or fail.
Once a write completes, later reads must reflect it or a newer write.
After communication returns, the system exchanges changes. It needs a rule to merge them, select one, or ask someone to resolve the conflict.
A database can offer different read guarantees. Choose for the operation rather than assuming every request has the same behavior.
It does not predict normal-operation latency, capacity or operating cost; evaluate those separately.
